title: The Bakery's Last Hour
passage:
On Saturday mornings, a bakery near Sota's house sold bread at a lower price just before closing. Sota had always thought the bakery was simply trying to sell everything before the food became old. One day, however, he saw a poster explaining that the shop was also working to reduce food waste. Sota became curious and asked the owner how much bread was usually left at the end of the day. The owner said that the amount changed depending on the weather, holidays, and local events. If the shop made too little bread, customers were disappointed. If it made too much, some bread remained unsold. The bakery had tried several ways to solve the problem. First, the staff kept detailed records of sales. They learned that rainy afternoons usually meant fewer customers, while school events could suddenly increase demand. Second, they made smaller amounts of some products and baked additional bread later when necessary. Finally, they offered discount bags near closing time. Sota asked whether discounts caused people to wait until the end of the day instead of buying bread at the normal price. The owner said this sometimes happened, but not often enough to create a serious problem. Most customers wanted a particular kind of bread at a convenient time. The discount bags contained whatever was left, so buyers could not choose everything. For a school project, Sota compared this system with food waste at home. He realized that families also had to make small predictions: how much rice to cook, which vegetables to use first, and when to freeze extra food. His family started writing the date on containers and placing older food at the front of the refrigerator. After two weeks, they checked their trash and noticed that they were throwing away much less food. Sota also learned that reducing waste did not always require a large new machine or an expensive service. Better information and a few flexible habits could make a difference. The bakery had taught him that waste is often connected with uncertainty about the future, and careful records can help people make better everyday decisions.

The bakery owner later showed Sota one more record: some products sold differently in winter and summer. That reminded him that useful data must be updated. A good rule from one season may fail in another, so reducing waste requires continued observation rather than a single permanent answer. This mattered too.
translation:
颯太の家の近くのパン屋では、土曜日の閉店前になるとパンを安く売っていました。颯太は、古くなる前に売り切りたいだけだと思っていましたが、ある日、食品ロス削減の取り組みだと書かれたポスターを見つけます。店主に尋ねると、売れ残る量は天気、休日、地域行事によって大きく変わることが分かりました。少なく作れば買えない客が出て、多く作れば余ってしまいます。そこで店は、販売記録を細かく残し、雨の日は客が減ることや学校行事の日は需要が増えることを学びました。また、一度に作る量を減らし、必要なら後から追加で焼くようにしました。閉店前の割引袋もその工夫の一つです。割引を待つ客が増えないかと颯太が尋ねると、多少はいても大きな問題ではなく、多くの客は好きなパンを都合のよい時間に買いたいのだと店主は説明しました。割引袋は残ったパンの組み合わせなので、自由に選べないからです。学校の課題で颯太は家庭の食品ロスにも目を向けました。ご飯をどれだけ炊くか、どの野菜を先に使うか、余った物をいつ冷凍するかも小さな予測です。家族は容器に日付を書き、古い食品を冷蔵庫の手前に置くようにしました。二週間後、捨てる食品は明らかに減っていました。颯太は、食品ロスを減らすのに大きな機械や高価なサービスが必ずしも必要ではなく、情報と柔軟な習慣が役立つと学びます。無駄は未来を正確に予測できないことから生まれる場合があり、丁寧な記録が日々の判断を助けるのです。

店主はさらに、季節によって売れ方が変わる商品もあると記録を見せました。颯太は、役立つデータも更新が必要だと気づきます。ある季節にうまくいったルールが別の季節には合わないことがあるため、食品ロス削減には一度の答えではなく観察の継続が必要です。 この点も重要でした。
